courses.title: AI for Everyone
courses.description: A friendly introduction to AI for people with no technical background.

lessons.title: Core Concepts
lessons.summary: Understand what AI is, how it works, and where you already use it every day.

cards.title: Does AI actually understand what I say?
cards.body: AI does not understand like a person. It finds patterns in language, images, or data and predicts a useful response based on what it has learned.
cards.takeaway: AI predicts — it does not understand.

cards.title: Why does AI sometimes sound so confident?
cards.body: AI is designed to produce fluent answers, not to feel certainty. It may sound confident even when it is wrong, so important answers should be checked.
cards.takeaway: Fluency is not accuracy — always verify important answers.

cards.title: What makes today's AI different from older software?
cards.body: Older software follows exact rules written by humans. Modern AI learns patterns from examples, so it can handle flexible tasks like writing, summarizing, and recognizing images.
cards.takeaway: Modern AI learns from examples, not just rules.

cards.title: Where do I already use AI every day?
cards.body: You likely use AI in maps, search engines, shopping recommendations, spam filters, voice assistants, translation tools, and photo apps. Much of it works quietly in the background.
cards.takeaway: AI is already woven into your daily tools.

cards.title: What is a prompt?
cards.body: A prompt is the instruction or question you give to an AI tool. Clear prompts usually produce clearer answers because they give the AI better direction.
cards.takeaway: Clear prompts lead to clearer answers.

cards.title: What is a good first AI habit?
cards.body: Ask AI to explain its reasoning, list assumptions, or show alternatives. This turns AI from an answer machine into a thinking partner.
cards.takeaway: Ask for reasoning, not just answers.

lessons.title: Common Questions
lessons.summary: Get honest answers to the questions most people have when starting with AI.

cards.title: Can AI replace my own judgment?
cards.body: AI can support your thinking, but it should not replace your judgment. Use it to explore ideas, compare options, and draft work, then decide what makes sense.
cards.takeaway: AI supports judgment — it does not replace it.

cards.title: Is it safe to share personal information with AI?
cards.body: Avoid sharing passwords, private financial details, medical records, or sensitive personal information unless you fully trust the tool and understand its privacy rules.
cards.takeaway: Protect sensitive information — read the privacy rules first.

cards.title: Why does AI give different answers sometimes?
cards.body: AI can respond differently because it generates answers instead of retrieving one fixed response. Small changes in wording can lead to different wording, emphasis, or suggestions.
cards.takeaway: AI generates — small changes in input change the output.

cards.title: Can AI help me learn faster?
cards.body: Yes, AI can explain topics, quiz you, simplify text, and create examples. It works best when you ask follow-up questions and check important facts.
cards.takeaway: AI accelerates learning when you stay curious and verify.

cards.title: Do I need technical skills to use AI?
cards.body: No, many AI tools are built for everyday language. You can start by asking for summaries, explanations, drafts, plans, or comparisons.
cards.takeaway: Plain language is enough to get started.

cards.title: What should I try first with AI?
cards.body: Start with a low-risk task like summarizing an article, rewriting an email, planning a trip, or explaining a confusing term. Practice matters more than perfect prompts.
cards.takeaway: Start small — practice builds skill faster than theory.

lessons.title: Analogies & Myths
lessons.summary: Use everyday comparisons to understand AI — and clear up the most common misconceptions.

cards.title: How should I think about AI assistants?
cards.body: Think of an AI assistant as a helpful first draft partner. It can get you started, but you still review, edit, and decide. It is like a GPS: useful for directions, but you still watch the road.
cards.takeaway: AI is a starting point — you still drive.

cards.title: Why does AI need clear instructions?
cards.body: AI performs better when you explain the goal, audience, and format. Vague requests often lead to vague results. It is like ordering food: the clearer your order, the closer the result matches what you wanted.
cards.takeaway: Clarity in — clarity out.

cards.title: How can AI be useful but imperfect?
cards.body: AI can save time and suggest useful ideas, but it can also miss context or make mistakes. It is like a calculator with a sticky key: powerful, but you still check the result.
cards.takeaway: Useful does not mean flawless.

cards.title: Is AI always objective?
cards.body: No, AI can reflect patterns, gaps, or bias in the data used to train it. A polished answer is not automatically fair or complete.
cards.takeaway: Polish is not the same as objectivity.

cards.title: Does AI know the truth automatically?
cards.body: No, AI predicts likely answers and may be outdated or mistaken. For important topics, compare with trusted sources.
cards.takeaway: Verify before trusting — especially on important topics.

courses.title: Build Your First AI Agent
courses.description: Learn what AI agents are, how they work, and how to design one safely.

lessons.title: Agent Basics
lessons.summary: Understand what an AI agent is and how it differs from a regular chatbot.

cards.title: What is an AI agent?
cards.body: An AI agent is a system that uses AI to work toward a goal. Instead of only answering one message, it can follow steps, use tools, and check progress.
cards.takeaway: An agent is AI working toward a goal.

cards.title: How is an agent different from a chatbot?
cards.body: A chatbot usually responds to what you type. An agent can take a goal, decide the next step, use a tool, and keep going until the task is done or needs help.
cards.takeaway: Chatbots respond; agents work through steps.

cards.title: What makes agents useful?
cards.body: Agents are useful when a task has repeated steps, clear inputs, and a result you can review. They can help with research, summaries, planning, support, and routine operations.
cards.takeaway: Agents fit tasks with steps and reviewable results.

cards.title: What does autonomy mean?
cards.body: Autonomy means the agent can make some decisions about what to do next. More autonomy can save time, but it also needs clearer rules and stronger review.
cards.takeaway: More autonomy needs stronger guardrails.

cards.title: What is a simple agent example?
cards.body: A meeting-notes agent could read notes, find decisions, list action items, and draft a follow-up message. A person still checks the message before sending.
cards.takeaway: Simple agents turn messy input into useful output.

cards.title: Why start with one task?
cards.body: One focused task is easier to describe, test, and improve. A broad agent can become confusing because success is not clear.
cards.takeaway: One clear task is the best starting point.

cards.title: What can go wrong?
cards.body: An agent can misunderstand the goal, use the wrong information, skip a step, or take an action too soon. That is why beginners should keep human review in the loop.
cards.takeaway: Agents need review before important actions.

cards.title: What should a beginner remember?
cards.body: An agent is not magic. It is a workflow with AI inside it. The clearer the task, tools, and approval rules, the more useful the agent becomes.
cards.takeaway: Good agents come from good workflow design.

lessons.title: Goals, Tools, and Actions
lessons.summary: Learn the core building blocks every useful AI agent needs.

cards.title: What is an agent goal?
cards.body: The goal tells the agent what outcome to work toward. A strong goal is specific, useful, and easy to check when the work is finished.
cards.takeaway: A good goal is specific and checkable.

cards.title: What are agent instructions?
cards.body: Instructions tell the agent how to behave. They can define the role, steps, tone, limits, output format, and when the agent should ask for help.
cards.takeaway: Instructions turn a goal into behavior.

cards.title: What are tools?
cards.body: Tools let an agent do things beyond writing text. A tool might search the web, read a file, update a spreadsheet, send an email, or call an app.
cards.takeaway: Tools give agents real abilities.

cards.title: What are actions?
cards.body: Actions are the things an agent does with tools or outputs. Drafting a reply, creating a task, searching a source, and updating a record are all actions.
cards.takeaway: Actions are how agents move work forward.

cards.title: Why do agents need inputs?
cards.body: Inputs give the agent the information it needs to start. Inputs can be a message, file, form, customer request, meeting note, or database record.
cards.takeaway: Better inputs make better agent work possible.

cards.title: What is an output format?
cards.body: The output format tells the agent how to present the result. It might be a list, table, email draft, JSON object, checklist, or short summary.
cards.takeaway: Output format makes results easier to use.

cards.title: Why define limits?
cards.body: Limits tell the agent what not to do. For example, do not send emails, do not invent facts, do not use private data, or ask before changing records.
cards.takeaway: Limits keep agent behavior safer.

cards.title: What makes a tool safe to use?
cards.body: A safer tool has clear permissions, visible results, and a way for humans to approve important changes. Tools that change money, accounts, or private data need extra care.
cards.takeaway: Powerful tools need careful permissions.

lessons.title: Agent Workflows
lessons.summary: See how agents plan, act, check results, and improve through feedback.

cards.title: What is an agent workflow?
cards.body: An agent workflow is the path from request to result. It includes the trigger, input, steps, tools, checks, approvals, and final output.
cards.takeaway: A workflow shows how the agent gets work done.

cards.title: What is a trigger?
cards.body: A trigger is what starts the agent. It could be a button click, new email, uploaded file, form submission, schedule, or manual request.
cards.takeaway: The trigger starts the agent workflow.

cards.title: How does an agent plan?
cards.body: Planning means the agent breaks the goal into smaller steps. Simple agents may follow fixed steps, while more advanced agents may choose steps based on the situation.
cards.takeaway: Planning turns a goal into steps.

cards.title: How does an agent act?
cards.body: The agent acts by using tools or producing outputs. It might search, read, draft, summarize, compare, classify, or create a next-step recommendation.
cards.takeaway: Actions are the workflow steps in motion.

cards.title: Why should an agent check its work?
cards.body: Checking helps catch missing information, weak evidence, wrong format, or risky actions. A good workflow includes at least one review step before the final result.
cards.takeaway: Checking turns output into trustworthy work.

cards.title: What is a retry?
cards.body: A retry happens when the agent notices a problem and tries again. For example, if search results are weak, it can search with better keywords.
cards.takeaway: Retries help agents recover from weak results.

cards.title: What is human-in-the-loop?
cards.body: Human-in-the-loop means a person reviews or approves important steps. This is especially useful before sending messages, changing data, or making decisions.
cards.takeaway: Human review keeps important steps controlled.

cards.title: How do you improve a workflow?
cards.body: Watch where the agent fails, then adjust the inputs, instructions, tools, examples, or approval steps. Agent design improves through testing.
cards.takeaway: Better workflows come from testing and revision.

lessons.title: Human Approval and Safety
lessons.summary: Learn when agents should ask permission and how to avoid risky mistakes.

cards.title: Why does safety matter for agents?
cards.body: Agents can do more than answer questions, so mistakes can have real effects. Safety rules help prevent wrong actions, privacy leaks, and confusing results.
cards.takeaway: More action means more need for safety.

cards.title: When should an agent ask first?
cards.body: An agent should ask before sending messages, deleting files, spending money, changing records, sharing private data, or making high-impact recommendations.
cards.takeaway: Ask before important or irreversible actions.

cards.title: What data should stay protected?
cards.body: Protect passwords, financial details, health information, customer data, private documents, contracts, and anything confidential to a person or business.
cards.takeaway: Private data needs strict boundaries.

cards.title: What is a guardrail?
cards.body: A guardrail is a rule that limits what the agent can do. Guardrails can block unsafe requests, require approval, restrict tools, or force the agent to cite sources.
cards.takeaway: Guardrails define what the agent must not do.

cards.title: Why should agents show their work?
cards.body: Showing sources, assumptions, or steps makes it easier for humans to review the result. It also helps you spot when the agent skipped something important.
cards.takeaway: Visible reasoning makes review easier.

cards.title: What is a safe first agent?
cards.body: A safe first agent suggests or drafts work instead of taking final action. For example, it can draft an email but wait for you to send it.
cards.takeaway: Draft-first agents are safer for beginners.

cards.title: What should agents do when unsure?
cards.body: A good agent should say when it is missing information, ask a clarifying question, or stop instead of guessing. Guessing can create confident mistakes.
cards.takeaway: Good agents ask instead of guessing.

cards.title: How do you test safety?
cards.body: Test normal cases, messy cases, and unsafe requests. Make sure the agent succeeds when it should and refuses or asks for help when it should.
cards.takeaway: Test both success and refusal behavior.

lessons.title: Design Your First Agent
lessons.summary: Use a simple template to design a useful agent for one real task.

cards.title: Step 1: Pick one task
cards.body: Choose one repeated task that is annoying, low-risk, and easy to review. Good examples include summarizing notes, drafting replies, or organizing research.
cards.takeaway: Start with one repeated, low-risk task.

cards.title: Step 2: Define success
cards.body: Write what a good result looks like. Success could mean a clear summary, accurate action list, clean table, or draft that only needs light editing.
cards.takeaway: Define success before building the agent.

cards.title: Step 3: List the inputs
cards.body: Name what the agent needs to begin. This might be meeting notes, customer questions, a document, a form, or a folder of research links.
cards.takeaway: Inputs tell the agent where to start.

cards.title: Step 4: Choose tools
cards.body: Pick only the tools needed for the task. A first agent may need no tools beyond reading text and drafting output. Add more tools later.
cards.takeaway: Use the fewest tools that can solve the task.

cards.title: Step 5: Write instructions
cards.body: Tell the agent its role, goal, steps, limits, tone, and output format. Clear instructions make behavior easier to predict.
cards.takeaway: Role, goal, steps, limits, and format guide the agent.

cards.title: Step 6: Add approval points
cards.body: Decide where a human should review the work. Approval is especially important before sending, publishing, deleting, buying, or changing records.
cards.takeaway: Approval points control risky steps.

cards.title: Step 7: Test examples
cards.body: Run the agent on at least three realistic examples. Include one easy case, one messy case, and one case where the agent should ask for help.
cards.takeaway: Three test cases reveal what to improve.

cards.title: Step 8: Improve the agent
cards.body: Use test results to update the instructions, examples, tools, and safety rules. A useful agent gets better through small revisions.
cards.takeaway: Agent design improves one test at a time.

courses.title: Create Your First AI Skill
courses.description: Step-by-step: build a reusable AI skill for any repeated task in 5 minutes.

lessons.title: Skill Concepts
lessons.summary: Understand what an AI skill is and why reusable instructions save time.

cards.title: What is an AI skill?
cards.body: An AI skill is a reusable set of instructions for doing a specific task well. It helps AI repeat a workflow consistently instead of being re-explained each time.
cards.takeaway: A skill is a reusable instruction set for a repeated task.

cards.title: How is a skill different from a prompt?
cards.body: A prompt is usually a one-time instruction. A skill is packaged guidance that can be reused whenever the same type of task appears.
cards.takeaway: Prompts are one-off — skills are reusable.

cards.title: What should my first skill do?
cards.body: Your first skill should solve one repeated task, such as rewriting emails, summarizing calls, creating reports, or formatting notes. Keep it specific and easy to test.
cards.takeaway: One repeated task, specific and testable.

cards.title: What goes inside a useful skill?
cards.body: A useful skill includes purpose, steps, style preferences, output format, examples, and limits. These details help the AI produce consistent results.
cards.takeaway: Purpose + steps + format + examples = useful skill.

cards.title: Why do skills improve consistency?
cards.body: Skills reduce the need to remember every instruction each time. They give the AI a stable way to approach the same task repeatedly.
cards.takeaway: Skills create reliable, repeatable AI behavior.

cards.title: What is the easiest skill template?
cards.body: Use a simple structure: purpose, when to use it, steps to follow, output format, examples, and what to avoid. That is enough for many beginner skills.
cards.takeaway: Purpose, steps, format, examples, limits — that is your template.

lessons.title: Building Your Skill
lessons.summary: Practical answers for writing, testing, and improving your first skill.

cards.title: Do I need to code a skill?
cards.body: Not always. Many skills can start as plain-language instructions, examples, and a clear workflow, especially for writing, analysis, or formatting tasks.
cards.takeaway: Plain language is enough to start.

cards.title: How do I test my first skill?
cards.body: Run the skill on three real examples and check whether the output matches your expectations. Then adjust instructions where the result was unclear or inconsistent.
cards.takeaway: Three real examples reveal what to fix.

cards.title: Can one skill handle many tasks?
cards.body: It can, but beginners should avoid making one skill too broad. Smaller skills are easier to understand, test, reuse, and improve.
cards.takeaway: Narrow skills are easier to trust and improve.

cards.title: What makes a skill reusable?
cards.body: A skill is reusable when it describes a repeatable process, not just one situation. It should work across similar inputs without rewriting the instructions.
cards.takeaway: Describe the process, not just the situation.

cards.title: When should I update a skill?
cards.body: Update a skill when outputs are inconsistent, your workflow changes, or users keep correcting the same issue. Skills should improve through real use.
cards.takeaway: Real use reveals what needs updating.

lessons.title: Analogies & Myths
lessons.summary: Use clear comparisons to understand skills — and avoid common mistakes.

cards.title: How should I think about a skill?
cards.body: A skill teaches AI your preferred way to complete a task. It turns repeated instructions into a reusable pattern. It is like saving a recipe so you do not explain the dish from scratch every time.
cards.takeaway: Save the recipe — don't explain it every time.

cards.title: Why should a skill have examples?
cards.body: Examples show the AI what good output looks like. They reduce confusion when instructions could be interpreted in different ways. It is like showing a tailor a sample shirt instead of only describing the fit.
cards.takeaway: Show what good looks like — don't just describe it.

cards.title: Why keep a skill focused?
cards.body: Focused skills are easier for AI to follow and for you to evaluate. Too many goals can make the output messy. It is like labeling one drawer for one category instead of stuffing everything inside.
cards.takeaway: One drawer, one category — one skill, one job.

cards.title: Is a skill the same as automation?
cards.body: No, a skill describes how AI should perform a task. Automation connects that task to triggers, apps, or workflows that run it.
cards.takeaway: Skills define the how — automation handles the when.

cards.title: Will a skill work perfectly forever?
cards.body: No, skills need review as tools, workflows, and expectations change. Treat them as living instructions, not finished documents.
cards.takeaway: Skills are living documents — update them as you grow.

courses.title: Prompt Engineering 101
courses.description: Learn how to ask AI better questions, give useful context, and improve answers through iteration.

lessons.title: Prompt Foundations
lessons.summary: Understand prompts, context, examples, and the habits that make AI easier to work with.

cards.title: What is prompt engineering?
cards.body: Prompt engineering means designing and improving the instructions you give an AI model so it better understands your goal and produces the kind of answer you want.
cards.takeaway: Better prompts guide AI toward better answers.

cards.title: What counts as a prompt?
cards.body: A prompt is the input you give AI. It can be a simple question, a direct command, a set of steps, an example, a code snippet, or background information.
cards.takeaway: A prompt is any input that guides the AI response.

cards.title: Why does context matter?
cards.body: Context helps AI understand the situation, audience, purpose, and constraints. Without context, the model has to guess what matters.
cards.takeaway: Context reduces guesswork.

cards.title: How do examples improve prompts?
cards.body: Examples show the AI the pattern you want. One example can guide style, and several examples can teach format, tone, level of detail, or structure.
cards.takeaway: Examples show what good output looks like.

cards.title: What is zero-shot prompting?
cards.body: Zero-shot prompting means asking directly without giving examples. It works well for simple tasks like summarizing, translating, listing ideas, or answering clear questions.
cards.takeaway: Zero-shot means direct instruction, no examples.

cards.title: What is few-shot prompting?
cards.body: Few-shot prompting means giving a few input-output examples before the real request. This helps AI copy the pattern and produce a more predictable response.
cards.takeaway: Few-shot prompting teaches by example.

cards.title: How do you make a prompt specific?
cards.body: Use action verbs, define the output format, name the audience, include important background, and break complex work into smaller steps.
cards.takeaway: Specific prompts give AI a clearer target.

cards.title: Why should you iterate?
cards.body: Prompting is a cycle. Read the result, notice what is missing or unclear, then revise your prompt with more context, examples, limits, or format instructions.
cards.takeaway: Prompting improves through feedback and revision.

lessons.title: Context and Examples
lessons.summary: Use roles, goals, constraints, and examples to guide AI toward more useful answers.

cards.title: Why does context change the answer?
cards.body: AI responds based on the information you provide. If you explain the goal, audience, format, and constraints, the answer can become much more relevant.
cards.takeaway: Better context creates better answers.

cards.title: What does a role do in a prompt?
cards.body: A role tells AI what perspective to use, such as tutor, editor, coach, analyst, or planner. It helps shape tone and focus.
cards.takeaway: Roles guide the perspective.

cards.title: Why mention the audience?
cards.body: The same topic should sound different for beginners, customers, investors, students, or teammates. Naming the audience helps AI choose the right level.
cards.takeaway: Audience controls the level.

cards.title: How do examples help?
cards.body: Examples show AI the style, structure, or quality you want. A short example can be clearer than a long explanation.
cards.takeaway: Examples show the target.

cards.title: What are constraints?
cards.body: Constraints are limits such as length, tone, format, reading level, or things to avoid. They help AI produce something closer to your real need.
cards.takeaway: Constraints make output usable.

cards.title: What format should I request?
cards.body: Ask for bullets, a table, a checklist, a script, a summary, or step-by-step instructions when the format matters.
cards.takeaway: Ask for the shape you need.

cards.title: When should I provide source material?
cards.body: If accuracy matters, paste the relevant source text or facts. AI can then work from your material instead of guessing from general patterns.
cards.takeaway: Source material reduces guessing.

cards.title: What is a good context template?
cards.body: A simple template is: goal, audience, context, constraints, examples, and output format. You do not need every part every time.
cards.takeaway: Goal, audience, context, constraints, examples, format.

lessons.title: Iterate and Improve
lessons.summary: Turn rough AI output into better work by asking for revisions, checks, and alternatives.

cards.title: Why is the first answer rarely final?
cards.body: AI often gives a useful starting point, not a finished result. Treat the first answer like a draft you can shape.
cards.takeaway: The first answer is a draft.

cards.title: How do I ask for a better version?
cards.body: Name what should change: make it shorter, clearer, warmer, more specific, more practical, or more beginner-friendly.
cards.takeaway: Specific revision requests work best.

cards.title: Why ask AI to explain assumptions?
cards.body: Assumptions reveal what AI guessed. Once you see them, you can correct missing context or spot weak reasoning.
cards.takeaway: Assumptions reveal guesses.

cards.title: How can AI compare options?
cards.body: Ask for pros, cons, tradeoffs, and a recommendation. This is helpful when you need to make a decision, not just get text.
cards.takeaway: Comparison helps decisions.

cards.title: What does it mean to critique output?
cards.body: You can ask AI to review its own answer for gaps, unclear claims, missing steps, or risks. Then use that critique to improve the result.
cards.takeaway: Critique before you trust.

cards.title: How do I avoid generic output?
cards.body: Add details about your situation, voice, audience, and real constraints. Generic prompts often create generic answers.
cards.takeaway: Specific inputs beat generic prompts.

cards.title: When should I restart instead of revise?
cards.body: If an answer goes in the wrong direction, rewrite the prompt with clearer context instead of trying to patch every issue.
cards.takeaway: Restart when the direction is wrong.

cards.title: What is the best prompting habit?
cards.body: Keep a small library of prompts that work for repeated tasks. Improve them over time as you learn what produces useful results.
cards.takeaway: Save and improve prompts that work.

courses.title: Vibe Coding for Non-Technical Builders
courses.description: Learn how to turn ideas into simple apps and websites with AI, even if you do not code.

lessons.title: Vibe Coding Basics
lessons.summary: Understand what vibe coding is, what AI can build, and how to start safely.

cards.title: What is vibe coding?
cards.body: Vibe coding means describing what you want in plain language and using AI to help create, edit, and test code. You guide the direction while AI handles much of the technical typing.
cards.takeaway: You guide the idea; AI helps with the code.

cards.title: Do I need to know programming first?
cards.body: You do not need to be a professional developer, but you do need to describe goals clearly, test carefully, and learn basic product logic.
cards.takeaway: No coding background required, but testing matters.

cards.title: What can I build first?
cards.body: Start with a simple landing page, calculator, quiz, checklist, tracker, or small internal tool. Small projects teach faster.
cards.takeaway: Small apps are the best first projects.

cards.title: What is the builder's job?
cards.body: Your job is to explain the user, the goal, the workflow, and what good looks like. AI needs direction to build the right thing.
cards.takeaway: Define the product before asking for code.

cards.title: Why should I avoid huge first builds?
cards.body: Big apps hide too many decisions. A small version helps you learn what users need and what the app should do next.
cards.takeaway: Build the smallest useful version first.

cards.title: What should I test?
cards.body: Click every button, try empty fields, use wrong inputs, resize the screen, and make sure the main workflow actually works.
cards.takeaway: Testing is part of building.

cards.title: What is a good AI coding prompt?
cards.body: Describe the goal, target user, pages, actions, data, visual style, and success criteria. Then ask AI to implement one step at a time.
cards.takeaway: Ask for one clear build step at a time.

cards.title: What should beginners remember?
cards.body: AI can move fast, but you still own the result. Review, test, simplify, and keep learning the basics as you build.
cards.takeaway: Fast building still needs careful review.

lessons.title: Plan Your First Build
lessons.summary: Turn a loose idea into screens, user flows, and a first version AI can help build.

cards.title: What problem does the app solve?
cards.body: Start by writing one sentence: this app helps this person do this task. If that sentence is unclear, the build will drift.
cards.takeaway: One clear problem keeps the build focused.

cards.title: Who is the user?
cards.body: Describe the person using the app, what they know, what they need, and what might confuse them.
cards.takeaway: Clear users create clear product decisions.

cards.title: What is the main workflow?
cards.body: Write the path a user takes from opening the app to getting value. This becomes your build checklist.
cards.takeaway: Workflow first, decoration later.

cards.title: How many screens do I need?
cards.body: Most first versions need fewer screens than you think. Start with the screens required for the main workflow.
cards.takeaway: Fewer screens are easier to finish.

cards.title: What data does the app need?
cards.body: List the information users enter, what the app stores, and what the app displays back.
cards.takeaway: Data shapes the app.

cards.title: What should the app not do yet?
cards.body: Write a short not-now list. This protects the first version from becoming too large.
cards.takeaway: A not-now list protects focus.

cards.title: How do I describe visual style?
cards.body: Use practical words like calm, playful, professional, minimal, dense, editorial, or mobile-first. Mention examples only if they help.
cards.takeaway: Style words guide the interface.

cards.title: What is done?
cards.body: Define done as a testable outcome: a user can complete the main workflow without confusion or broken buttons.
cards.takeaway: Done means the workflow works.

lessons.title: Test and Ship
lessons.summary: Learn the beginner-friendly checklist for reviewing AI-built apps before sharing them.

cards.title: Why test before sharing?
cards.body: AI-built apps can look finished while hiding broken states. Testing protects users and your credibility.
cards.takeaway: A polished look is not enough.

cards.title: What is a happy path test?
cards.body: A happy path test checks the normal user flow from start to finish. It answers: can the app do the main thing?
cards.takeaway: Happy path tests the main thing.

cards.title: What is an edge case?
cards.body: An edge case is something unusual but possible, like empty input, long text, slow loading, or a user tapping twice.
cards.takeaway: Edge cases reveal fragile spots.

cards.title: Why test on mobile?
cards.body: Many layouts that look good on desktop can break on a phone. Always check small screens if real users may use them.
cards.takeaway: Mobile testing catches layout problems.

cards.title: What should I ask AI to fix?
cards.body: Give AI the exact issue, what you expected, what happened, and where it happened. Screenshots and error messages help.
cards.takeaway: Specific bug reports get better fixes.

cards.title: How do I avoid breaking working features?
cards.body: After a fix, retest the main workflow. A change in one place can accidentally affect another place.
cards.takeaway: Retest after every important fix.

cards.title: When is it ready to share?
cards.body: Share when the main workflow works, content is clear, errors are handled, and the app feels understandable to a new user.
cards.takeaway: Ready means usable by someone new.

cards.title: What should I improve after launch?
cards.body: Watch where users get confused, what they repeat, and what they request. Let real use guide the next version.
cards.takeaway: User behavior guides version two.

courses.title: AI for Professionals
courses.description: Use AI to work smarter, communicate better, and automate the routine.

lessons.title: Professional Foundations
lessons.summary: Learn where AI fits in professional work and how to use it without losing your voice.

cards.title: Where can professionals use AI immediately?
cards.body: AI can help with emails, summaries, research, meeting notes, reports, brainstorming, spreadsheets, presentations, and planning. Start with tasks you repeat every week.
cards.takeaway: Start with your most repeated weekly tasks.

cards.title: What makes a prompt useful at work?
cards.body: A useful prompt includes context, goal, audience, tone, format, and constraints. The more clearly you define the job, the better the result usually becomes.
cards.takeaway: Context + goal + format = a useful work prompt.

cards.title: How can AI improve writing?
cards.body: AI can draft, rewrite, shorten, clarify, change tone, and create outlines. You should still review for accuracy, voice, and workplace sensitivity.
cards.takeaway: AI handles structure — you handle accuracy and voice.

cards.title: How can AI support better meetings?
cards.body: AI can turn notes into summaries, decisions, risks, and action items. It can also help prepare agendas and follow-up messages.
cards.takeaway: AI turns messy notes into clean action.

cards.title: What is workflow thinking with AI?
cards.body: Workflow thinking means placing AI inside a real work process, not using it as a random chatbot. This helps turn outputs into finished work.
cards.takeaway: Embed AI in the workflow — don't treat it as a chatbot.

cards.title: What is a personal AI playbook?
cards.body: A personal AI playbook is a short list of prompts and workflows you reuse. It helps you save time consistently instead of starting from zero.
cards.takeaway: Save your best prompts — reuse them every week.

lessons.title: Professional FAQs
lessons.summary: Answers to the questions professionals ask most about using AI responsibly at work.

cards.title: Can AI write my emails for me?
cards.body: AI can draft emails, but you should check tone, facts, names, and intent. The best results still sound like you and match the situation.
cards.takeaway: AI drafts — you review, personalize, and send.

cards.title: How do I avoid generic AI output?
cards.body: Give AI specific context, examples, audience details, and your preferred tone. Ask it to revise toward a clearer goal instead of accepting the first answer.
cards.takeaway: Specific input produces specific output.

cards.title: Can I use AI with confidential work?
cards.body: Only use approved tools and follow your organization's data rules. Avoid pasting confidential documents, customer data, or internal strategy into unapproved AI systems.
cards.takeaway: Approved tools only — know your organization's rules.

cards.title: How can managers use AI responsibly?
cards.body: Managers can use AI for planning, summarizing, communication, and analysis while keeping human judgment in decisions about people, performance, and sensitive issues.
cards.takeaway: AI supports analysis — humans own people decisions.

cards.title: Will AI make my work less personal?
cards.body: It can if you use raw outputs without editing. Use AI to handle structure and first drafts, then add judgment, context, and your own voice.
cards.takeaway: Add your voice after the AI draft.

cards.title: What should I automate first?
cards.body: Automate low-risk tasks that are repetitive, time-consuming, and easy to review. Good examples include summaries, formatting, status updates, and draft outlines.
cards.takeaway: Repetitive, low-risk, easy to review — automate those first.

lessons.title: Analogies & Myths
lessons.summary: Reframe how you think about AI at work — and clear up what it cannot do.

cards.title: How should I treat AI at work?
cards.body: Treat AI as a capable assistant, not a replacement for responsibility. It can speed up preparation, but you own the final result. It is like a junior colleague who drafts quickly but still needs your review.
cards.takeaway: You own the result — AI helps you prepare it.

cards.title: Why does AI need context?
cards.body: Without context, AI guesses what matters. With context, it can tailor the answer to your audience, goal, and situation. It is like asking for directions without saying where you are starting from.
cards.takeaway: No context means guesswork — give AI what it needs.

cards.title: How can AI reduce busywork?
cards.body: AI can handle first drafts and repetitive transformations, giving you more time for judgment and relationships. It is like a dishwasher: it saves labor, but you still decide what goes on the table.
cards.takeaway: AI handles the labor — you focus on the judgment.

cards.title: Does using AI mean I am cheating?
cards.body: Not when it is allowed, transparent when needed, and reviewed carefully. It is similar to using spellcheck, templates, or research tools responsibly.
cards.takeaway: Responsible use of tools is professional, not cheating.

cards.title: Can AI handle workplace nuance alone?
cards.body: No, AI can miss politics, emotions, history, and hidden context. Use it for support, but keep human judgment for delicate situations.
cards.takeaway: Nuance is yours — AI handles the structure.
